analysis.one_liner: Closes offshore tax loopholes used by corporations and wealthy individuals to shield income overseas.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by its sponsor and 56 Democratic cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote in either committee and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tighten a range of rules aimed at offshore tax avoidance. It would let the Treasury restrict foreign banks and countries that block U.S. tax enforcement, require public country-by-country reporting of profits and taxes by large corporations, tax companies managed from the United States as domestic companies, and limit the ability of U.S. firms to shift profits and intangibles like patents to low-tax affiliates. It would also tighten the rules for 'inversions,' in which a U.S. company acquires a foreign firm and reincorporates abroad to lower its tax bill.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who ultimately cover taxes that corporations and wealthy individuals shift offshore, plus honest domestic businesses that compete against rivals using offshore structures.

how_it_helps.text: Requires large public companies to publicly disclose revenues, profits, taxes paid, and employees on a country-by-country basis, making profit-shifting to tax havens visible [S2].

Treats foreign corporations managed and controlled primarily in the United States as domestic for tax purposes, and strengthens the rules against corporate inversions by lowering the ownership threshold and adding a management-and-control test [S2].

Creates rebuttable presumptions that money moved through entities in banks that refuse to report under FATCA is income of the U.S. person behind them, and lets Treasury impose restrictions on jurisdictions and institutions that significantly impede U.S. tax enforcement [S2].

Extends anti-money laundering duties to investment advisers and company formation agents, the professions used to build anonymous shell structures, and strengthens John Doe summons tools for IRS investigations [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations using offshore profit-shifting, wealthy individuals with hidden offshore accounts, offshore banks and company-formation services, and hedge funds and advisers using foreign structures, all of whom would face higher taxes or compliance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Multinationals, offshore banks, wealthy account holders

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes significant new reporting and compliance costs on financial institutions, investment advisers, company formation agents, and any U.S. business with foreign affiliates, including detailed country-by-country public disclosures [S2].

Its legal presumptions shift the burden of proof to taxpayers with offshore accounts at uncooperative institutions, who would need clear and convincing evidence to rebut the assumption that offshore funds are their unreported income [S3].

Critics of such measures argue that tightening U.S. corporate tax rules on foreign income can put American-headquartered firms at a disadvantage against foreign competitors, a cost that can ultimately fall on shareholders and workers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The revenue and fairness gains from curbing offshore avoidance are substantial, but the bill is broad and compliance-heavy, and some of its burden-shifting presumptions are aggressive. Its main cost falls on firms and investors using cross-border structures, which is the point of the bill; the honest trade-off is higher compliance costs across international finance in exchange for more enforceable taxation of offshore income.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two committees, but neither ever acted on it, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the Stop Tax Haven Abuse Act in the House on January 13, 2015, joined by 56 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded in the action history; the bill remained in committee until the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations, offshore financial institutions, and holders of undeclared offshore accounts are better off, since the tax and disclosure rules the bill would have imposed never became law.

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Paul Ryan, R-WI)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup appears in the action history.

against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the banking and securities provisions after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 57 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and the committees where the bill sat were controlled by Republicans; no roll-call was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would tax income shifted to low-tax affiliates, restrict deductions tied to deferred foreign income, and force public country-by-country reporting of profits and taxes [S2]. Its interest in avoiding those taxes comes at the direct expense of the tax base ordinary workers fund [S2].

Treasury could restrict correspondent accounts and payment cards of institutions that impede U.S. tax enforcement, and transactions with banks that refuse FATCA reporting would face adverse tax presumptions [S2][S3].
New beneficial-owner reporting and rebuttable presumptions that offshore funds are taxable income would sharply raise the risk and cost of hiding money abroad [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Company formation agents and investment advisers
industries.note: Both would be brought under anti-money laundering requirements, ending their role in creating anonymous offshore entities [S2].

industries.industry: Corporate inversion targets (accounting, legal, and advisory services)
industries.note: Tighter inversion rules would reduce the market for cross-border reincorporation deals, which the bill treats as primarily a tax-avoidance vehicle [S2].
